title: The Assessor of Mines: Longitude, Metallurgy, and the Spiritual Sense of Scripture
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Stockholm, Gamla Stan: the court chaplain's son
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 January 1688 Old Style. The Gregorian equivalent is 8 February, not the 9 February that swedenborg.com and several English sources give: the Julian-Gregorian offset in 1688 was ten days, and Swedish Wikipedia states the conversion outright. The Old Style date is used as the sort key because it is what Stockholm itself wrote. The birth house is not recorded in any reachable source, so the coordinate is a district anchor in the old town, near Stortorget, and is not a street address.
stops.campa: A son is born to Jesper Swedberg, court chaplain, and Sara Behm, daughter of an assessor of the Board of Mines. The house is not recorded; the old town is. His father preaches a Lutheranism crowded with angels and devils who interfere in daily business, and holds that the spiritual world presses on this one at every point. Nothing in that is figurative to the man saying it. His mother's family holds the mining office, and her son will hold it for thirty-one years, from 1716 until he petitions his way out of it at fifty-nine.
sources: sv.wikipedia, 'Emanuel Swedenborg', on the calendar conversion
suggested_refs: Gamla Stan, Stockholm, parish of the royal chapel in 1688

stops.name: Uppsala, the professor's house
stops.date_confidence: the family's move to Uppsala on Jesper Swedberg's professorship is dated 1692 in the Colegio Invisible dossier and is consistent with sv.wikipedia on his career, but I could not confirm the specific move date against an independent source in this pass. Treat the year as dossier-sourced. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The coordinate is Uppsala Cathedral, the town's fixed point; the professorial house itself is not identified.
stops.campa: Jesper Swedberg takes a chair of theology at Uppsala and brings his family north from the capital. Emanuel is four. The town is a cathedral, a university, and a river, and it will hold him for seventeen years. In this house, he writes much later, he thought continually about God and salvation and said things his parents took for the speech of angels through a child's mouth. The letter that reports it is written when he is seventy-one, and it is the only witness to any of it.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, from Sigstedt and Acton documentary material
suggested_refs: Uppsala under Jesper Swedberg's professorship, 1692-1702

stops.name: Uppsala, the eleven-year-old matriculant
stops.date_confidence: matriculation at eleven attested by swedenborg.com's life chronology; month and day are not given and default to 01-01. Sara Behm's death when he was eight, dated 1696, comes from the dossier citing Acton's Letters and Memorials and is not independently reverified here. The coordinate is the Gustavianum, the university's main building in this period.
stops.campa: Sara Behm dies when her son is eight. Three years later he is entered on the university rolls, an ordinary age for a boy of his class to begin. He reads Latin, Greek, Hebrew, mathematics, and the natural philosophy arriving out of England. The record of these years holds no visions and no prodigies, only a diligent boy in a house of clergy learning to construe. He does it in a building put up east of the cathedral seventy years before, under a dome with an anatomical theatre inside it, its tiers of benches ringing a dissection table.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, citing Acton, Letters and Memorials
suggested_refs: The Gustavianum at Uppsala, built 1622-25, with its anatomical theatre

stops.name: Uppsala, the librarian's household
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia documents his residence with Erik Benzelius the Younger as 1703-1709. The dossier and the geography lens both compressed this into a single span running from the family's 1692 arrival, which conflates two separate events; 1703 is used here and the conflation is flagged in the report. Jesper Swedberg's elevation to the see of Skara is attested to 1702 by sv.wikipedia. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: His father is made bishop of Skara and leaves for the west country. Emanuel stays behind in the house of his brother-in-law Erik Benzelius the Younger, librarian of the university, and remains there six years. Benzelius corresponds with half of learned Europe and keeps the library where the letters land. It is he, not the bishop, who turns the boy toward mathematics, mechanics, and the Latin republic of letters, and he to whom Swedenborg will write his questions from London a decade later.
sources: sv.wikipedia, on Jesper Swedberg's 1702 appointment to Skara
suggested_refs: The Uppsala University library under Erik Benzelius the Younger

stops.name: Uppsala, Gustavianum: Seneca and Publilius Syrus
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1709 by swedenborg.com's life chronology and by Wikipedia; the month is not given in either and defaults to 01. The work is an edition with commentary rather than an original dissertation in the modern sense, and sources describe it both ways without contradiction.
stops.campa: He finishes his course with a printed volume, an edition of moral maxims gathered out of Seneca and Publilius Syrus with notes of his own. It is a young Latinist's exercise in the ethics of endurance, and it is the first thing he publishes, forty years before he writes a line of theology. What he has at twenty-one is Latin, access to a press, and the habit of working line by line through another man's sentences until they hold. Everything else that will make him famous is still in front of him. Uppsala prints the volume in 1709, under the name Swedberg.
suggested_refs: Selectae sententiae L. Annaei Senecae et Publilii Syri mimi, Uppsala, 1709

stops.name: London, Crane Court: among the Newtonians
stops.date_confidence: the 1710 departure and the several London years are attested by Wikipedia; the month is not fixed and defaults to 01. The Crane Court coordinate is inherited byte-identical from newton.journey.json, where the Royal Society's 1710 purchase of the houses is documented; Swedenborg's presence in that milieu is dossier and standard-biography material, not an attendance record. The claim that he attended Newton's lectures rests on the Swedenborg Society's own biography and is marked [R] in the report.
stops.campa: He sails for England through a war and a quarantine and lands in a London where the Royal Society has just bought itself houses in Crane Court. He lodges with a watchmaker, then a cabinetmaker, then an instrument maker, taking each trade off his landlord by watching him work. He reads Newton and intends to meet him. That he actually attended Newton's lectures is asserted by his own society two centuries afterwards and by nobody at all who was in London at the time.
sources: Swedenborg Society, 'About Swedenborg' (for the Newton-lectures claim)
newton.journey.json, for the Crane Court coordinate
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's houses in Crane Court, Fleet Street, bought 1710

stops.name: Greenwich, the Astronomer Royal's tables
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The Royal Observatory and John Flamsteed's tenure are attested; Swedenborg's approach to him is the dossier's reading of his correspondence with Benzelius and was not confirmed against a primary document in this pass. Dated 1711 as a sort placeholder inside the documented 1710-1715 English stay. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from edmond_halley.journey.json.
stops.campa: Below the hill at Greenwich, John Flamsteed has spent thirty years measuring the sky to a standard nobody has matched, and Swedenborg wants his lunar observations. He has a method for finding longitude at sea from the moon's place among the fixed stars, and a method without tables is worth nothing. He writes to Benzelius about it from London. He will republish the longitude method for the next forty years and never win the prize. Whether Flamsteed ever received him, or answered him at all, is recorded nowhere the sources reach.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, from the Benzelius correspondence
suggested_refs: Flamsteed House and the lunar observations sought for the longitude method

stops.name: Amsterdam, the first of the returns
stops.date_confidence: the Netherlands leg of the grand tour is attested to the 1710-1715 span by Wikipedia without a precise year; 1713 orders the itinerary and is not a claim about the month or the day. The trades he learned in the Low Countries come from the dossier's synthesis. City-level coordinate; no lodging or press address is established.
stops.campa: He crosses to the Netherlands and finds the city that will print most of his life's work. Amsterdam has presses that answer to no Lutheran consistory, booksellers who ship anywhere, and no curiosity at all about what a foreign gentleman pays to have set in Latin. He learns lens-grinding here, and binding, and engraving. Half a century on, an old man with eight volumes of visions and a state church at his back, he will come back for exactly this advantage and use it until he dies.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, grand-tour itinerary and trades
suggested_refs: The Amsterdam book trade of the early eighteenth century

stops.name: Paris, the notebook of machines
stops.date_confidence: the Paris leg is attested at city level by the dossier's grand-tour synthesis; no specific sites of his stay are documented in sources reachable here. Dated 1714 to order the itinerary. The catalogue of unbuilt machines belongs to this period of his notebooks in the standard biographies rather than to a document dated at Paris.
stops.campa: Paris holds him through a season of academies and instrument shops. He is twenty-six and carrying a notebook of designs: a submarine, an air pump, a machine that plays music by mechanism, a flying machine. None of them is built. Engineers looking at the flying machine two centuries afterwards say the wing is sound and the power was never there to have. The sheet itself survives: a car slung under a rigid frame, with paddles for the pilot to beat down against the air using his own arms.
suggested_refs: Swedenborg's notebook designs for a flying machine and a submarine, c. 1714

segments.name: The Board of Mines and the Machine of the World

stops.name: Lund, the king and the assessorship
stops.date_confidence: the Lund meeting with Charles XII and the 1716 appointment as assessor extraordinary of the Bergskollegium are attested by Wikipedia; the month is not given and defaults to 01. The coordinate is Lund Cathedral, the town's central landmark, used because no specific meeting site is named in the sources. Daedalus Hyperboreus is attested to 1716-1718 and six issues by swedenborg.com and Wikipedia, which give no printing address; the periodical is folded into this stop rather than pinned separately.
stops.campa: Charles XII, home from five years as a Turkish guest and fighting a war he cannot win, receives the young man at Lund and appoints him assessor extraordinary of the Bergskollegium, the board that governs Sweden's mines and ironworks. The king likes mathematics and likes usefulness. Swedenborg is already printing Daedalus Hyperboreus, six issues carrying Christopher Polhem's machines and his own calculations to whoever in Sweden reads such things, and generally counted the first scientific periodical the country has had.
suggested_refs: Daedalus Hyperboreus, six issues, 1716-1718

stops.name: Trollhattan, the locks and Polhem's daughter
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The Emerentia Polhem episode is dated September 1718 by swedenborgdigitallibrary.org's Swedenborg Epic, which rests on a document produced to a Stockholm society only in 1789 and on Gabriel Polhem's late family testimony. The dossier itself flags that this is not evidence of a consummated engagement. The canal work with Polhem at Trollhattan is well attested; the courtship is tradition.
stops.campa: At the falls of Trollhattan he works with Christopher Polhem on locks meant to lift ships past the water, and falls in love with Polhem's second daughter Emerentia, who is fifteen. Polhem draws up a contract of future marriage. Her brother Gabriel takes the paper out of the house, seeing what she will not say to her father. Swedenborg relinquishes the claim and goes, and the whole account comes from a document laid before a Stockholm society in 1789, seventy years later. He never marries anyone.
suggested_refs: The lock works at the falls of Trollhattan, Polhem's canal project

stops.name: Fredriksten, the vessels overland and the shot in the trench
stops.date_confidence: Charles XII's death at the siege of Fredriksten is attested to November 1718 by Wikipedia; the pool gives the month only, so the day defaults to 01. Swedenborg's role in the overland ship transport is [R]: broadly grounded engineering fact per the dossier, inflated into a solo feat by later retelling. The coordinate is corrected from the research pool's 11.3861, which lands in Halden town some 400 metres west of the ramparts, to the fortress height at 59.1181, 11.3925 per en.wikipedia's listed position.
stops.campa: For the Norwegian campaign the engineers move vessels overland on rollers and prepared road, capstan by capstan, to bring them to water below the fortress. Swedenborg is one of them; later tellings hand him the whole feat alone. In November the king is killed by a shot in the forward trench at Fredriksten, and the absolutism, the campaign, the canal money and Daedalus Hyperboreus all end together inside a single season. He is thirty and has to start again in a country that now has a parliament.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, on the ship transport and its later exaggeration
suggested_refs: Fredriksten fortress above Halden, siege of 1718

stops.name: Stockholm, Riddarhuset: the new name
stops.date_confidence: the 1719 ennoblement by Ulrika Eleonora and the introduction at the House of Nobility are attested by swedenborg.com and Wikipedia; the month is not given and defaults to 01. The Riddarhuset coordinate is the building itself, per Wikipedia. That he spoke with difficulty is reported later rather than contemporaneously, and is carried here as report.
stops.campa: Queen Ulrika Eleonora ennobles the children of the late bishop, as bishops' families are ennobled, and Swedberg becomes Swedenborg. The siblings are introduced at the House of Nobility, and Emanuel takes the seat that comes with it in the Riksdag of the Age of Liberty, where he will sit for half a century among men arguing over currency, iron exports and the price of grain. He speaks with difficulty, by every later account, and prefers to put his arguments in writing and hand them in.
suggested_refs: The Riddarhuset, Stockholm, seat of the noble estate in the Age of Liberty

stops.name: Uppsala, the chair declined
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1724 by Wikipedia; month and day are not given and default to 01-01. The stammer is given in the sources as a later report, not as a contemporaneous statement by Swedenborg, and the dossier flags it as such.
stops.campa: Uppsala offers him the professorship of mathematics. He refuses it. He says the work he does at the Board of Mines is practical and various and would be spoiled by a lecture hall, and a later report adds that he stammered and did not want a room of students watching him try to speak. He is thirty-six. He has no wife and no household to keep, and the mines pay him a salary for work he arranges at his own hours. He stays at the Board another twenty-three years.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, on the stammer as later report
suggested_refs: The Uppsala chair of mathematics, declined 1724

stops.name: Dresden and Leipzig, the Opera philosophica et mineralia
stops.date_confidence: the 1734 three-volume publication at Dresden and Leipzig is attested by swedenborg.com and Wikipedia; the month is not given and defaults to 01. The coordinate is Dresden at city level; the specific presses are not established in sources reachable here, and the work was printed across both cities.
stops.campa: Three folio volumes come off the presses at once: the Principia rerum naturalium, deriving the world from a first natural point set in spiral motion, and two enormous practical volumes on iron and on copper and brass, their smelting and assaying, written by a man eighteen years inside the industry. The cosmology and the metallurgy are bound as one work because their author can see no seam between them. Reviewers take the metallurgy seriously and leave the cosmology where it lies.
suggested_refs: Opera philosophica et mineralia, 3 vols., Dresden and Leipzig, 1734

stops.name: Amsterdam, the economy of the animal kingdom
stops.date_confidence: swedenborg.com gives Oeconomia regni animalis as published 1740-1741 in two volumes at Amsterdam. The research pool's chronology lens gave the place as 'London, England / Amsterdam', which contradicts its own geography lens and the imprint; London does not belong here and is dropped. Month unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He has turned from the outside of nature to the inside of a body, and what he is looking for is the soul. Two volumes on the blood, the heart, the cortex and the fibre, compiled out of the best anatomists of Europe rather than from his own dissections, and reasoned upward: if the soul is anywhere it is in the organization, and organization can be read. He is fifty-two. The method is the one he used on iron ore: gather what the best observers report, and reason up from the structure to the cause. Amsterdam prints the first volume in 1740 and the second the year after.
suggested_refs: Oeconomia regni animalis, 2 vols., Amsterdam, 1740-41

stops.name: Stockholm, elected to the Academy of Sciences
stops.date_confidence: the 1740 election is confirmed by sv.wikipedia and carried by the dossier chronology; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The coordinate is a central Stockholm point and is deliberately not the Academy's modern Frescati premises at 59.3697, 18.0559, which were not built until 1915 and would be anachronistic for a 1740 election. In 1740 the Academy had no purpose-built home. The two lenses of the research pool gave both coordinates for the same institution; the split is resolved by dating, not by preference.
stops.campa: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences elects him a member in its founding decade, when it has no building of its own and meets where it can. He is the assessor of mines who published a cosmology, and by the standards of that room the combination is unremarkable. Thirty-two years from now his heirs will hand this same body some twenty thousand manuscript pages, and the Academy will keep them without ever taking a position on whether any of it is true. He is fifty-two and has published nothing anyone would call theology.
sources: UNESCO, 'Emanuel Swedenborg Collection', Memory of the World record
suggested_refs: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in its first decade, without fixed premises

stops.name: Stockholm, Hornsgatan: the house and the garden
stops.date_confidence: swedenborg.com's account of the garden gives acquisition in 1743 and occupancy from 1745, and lists the gate, orchard, kitchen garden, maze, birdhouse, library and summerhouse. The street is given, not a number. The coordinate is corrected from the research pool's 59.3172, 18.0672, which sits at the Slussen end of Sodermalm, westward to the Hornsgatan stretch by Mariatorget where the plot stood; it remains an approximation on that street.
stops.campa: On Hornsgatan, on the south island, he buys a plot with a wooden house, a workshop, and about an acre of ground, and moves into it two years later. He lays out an orchard, a kitchen garden, a hedge maze, a birdhouse, an ornate gate, and at the western end a small summerhouse of one room. Neighbours report that the gate stands open and that visitors are shown the garden by its owner, an elderly gentleman who is polite, lives alone, and keeps a gardener's family in the yard.
suggested_refs: The Hornsgatan property on Sodermalm, bought 1743, occupied from 1745

stops.name: Ystad, the road south
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The 21 July 1743 departure from Stockholm and the itinerary through Ystad, Stralsund, Hamburg, Bremen and the Netherlands come from the journal's own dated entries as presented at newchristianbiblestudy.org and relayed by the dossier; I did not re-verify against a scholarly edition. The stop is placed at Ystad, the Baltic crossing point, on the departure date. The 1859 first publication is dossier-sourced and is flagged in the report.
stops.campa: He leaves Stockholm on the twenty-first of July with leave from the Board of Mines and a book to write, and takes the road down through Sweden to Ystad and the Baltic crossing. In his baggage is a notebook kept for nobody, in which he begins recording the journey, the food, the state of his body, and then his dreams. He does not intend it to be read. It will be found in a Swedish library over a century later and printed, and it is the only place he ever writes about himself without arranging it first.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, citing the Journal of Dreams itinerary at newchristianbiblestudy.org
suggested_refs: The Dromboken, Swedenborg's private travel and dream journal, 1743-44

stops.name: The Hague, the animal kingdom continued
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Wikipedia attests Regnum animale to 1744 and gives the place as The Hague, with London also named in the pool for the continuation; the month is not given and defaults to 01. The Hague is also documented as one of his recurring European bases across the 1720s-1740s rather than as a single dated visit, so this stop carries both the imprint and the residence pattern.
stops.campa: The Animal Kingdom goes to press, the anatomical work continued and the search for the soul continued in it. He has planned seventeen parts. Three will appear. Through the same months the private notebook is filling with material of an entirely different order: a man weeping, trembling, thrown on his face, dreaming of women and of his father, waking convinced he has been in the presence of something. He writes both in the same rooms, in the same weeks, and dates the notebook entries as carefully as he dates the proofs. Nobody sees the notebook in his lifetime.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, on The Hague as a recurring base
suggested_refs: Regnum animale, The Hague, 1744, three parts of a projected seventeen

stops.name: Delft, the nights after Easter
stops.date_confidence: the crisis is attested to 6-7 April 1744 by Wikipedia. The place is corrected: the research pool's geography lens put this in London at 51.5074, -0.1278, contradicting its own chronology lens, which put it in the Netherlands; the standard reading of the journal places the vision at Delft, and Delft is used. The framing 'Easter weekend' is dropped, since Gregorian Easter Sunday 1744 fell on 5 April, making 6-7 April Easter Monday into Tuesday.
stops.campa: At Delft, in the nights of the sixth and seventh of April, the crisis comes to its point. He records trembling that throws him to the floor, a light, a sound like a wind, and then Christ present in the room, holding his hands, asking whether he has a clean bill of health. He answers that the Lord knows better than he does. He wakes changed and writes it down in Swedish, in a private notebook, in the same handwriting he uses for the state of his stomach. Easter Sunday that year had fallen on the fifth.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, on the Journal of Dreams
suggested_refs: The Journal of Dreams entries for 6-7 April 1744, National Library of Sweden

stops.name: London, the inn and the commission
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The fullest early source is Carl Robsahm's memoir, written and published after Swedenborg's death from later conversations, so the episode documents his own narrated self-understanding rather than an independently verified event. The year 1745 is what the sources give; no month or day, defaulted to 01-01. The inn is not named in anything reachable, so the coordinate is central London.
stops.campa: He is dining alone in a room at a London inn when a darkness comes over the food and he sees a man sitting in the corner of it, who tells him not to eat so much. He goes home frightened. The same figure returns in the night, says that he is God and Lord, and gives him a commission: to explain to men the spiritual sense of Scripture. From here he reads Hebrew, keeps the journal differently, and begins the work of the rest of his life. The only source for the scene is a banker's memoir written after his death.
sources: Carl Robsahm, Memoirs of Swedenborg, as characterized in the Colegio Invisible dossier
suggested_refs: Robsahm's Memoirs of Swedenborg, the earliest full account of the 1745 call

stops.name: Stockholm, released from the Board of Mines
stops.date_confidence: swedenborg.com gives the petition under 1747; Wikipedia gives the resignation as June 1747. The day is not given and defaults to 01. That the release was honourable and carried half salary as pension is attested by both, against the later story that he was dismissed. City-level coordinate for an administrative act.
stops.campa: He petitions to be relieved of his office after thirty-one years in it. The crown grants it honourably and gives him half his salary as a pension, which is what the record shows and not what the stories will later say. He is fifty-nine: financially independent, unmarried, unemployed, and about to start publishing anonymously in a foreign country. His colleagues at the Bergskollegium note the departure without remark. He goes on attending the Riksdag for another twenty years.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, from Acton's Letters and Memorials
suggested_refs: The Bergskollegium resignation memorials, June 1747

stops.name: London, Arcana Coelestia
stops.date_confidence: attested to London 1749-1756, eight quarto volumes, 4,559 pages, published anonymously and at his own cost, by swedenborg.com's writings chronology and by Wikipedia. Month not given, defaulted to 01. The specific London printer is not established in sources reachable here. The poor sales are attested; the exact first-year figure is not.
stops.campa: The first of eight quarto volumes appears in London with no author's name on it: a verse-by-verse reading of Genesis and Exodus through correspondences, where every literal word carries an inner sense, interleaved with reports of what he says he has been shown of heaven and hell. Four and a half thousand pages over seven years, printed at his own expense. The sales are negligible. He gives most of the run away to bishops, universities and libraries across Europe, and waits to see who writes back. No name appears on any of the eight title pages.
suggested_refs: Arcana Coelestia, 8 vols., London 1749-1756, published anonymously
The torn sections of these volumes carried and read aloud on Ohio floors by John Chapman, per johnny_appleseed.journey.json

stops.name: Stockholm, the summerhouse at the garden's end
stops.date_confidence: undated. 1752 is a sort placeholder inside the documented occupancy of the Hornsgatan property from 1745, chosen to sit between Arcana Coelestia and Heaven and Hell. The summerhouse and its use are attested by swedenborg.com; the visitors' descriptions of his manner and habits come from the dossier's synthesis of Tafel's collected testimony and are reports, not records.
stops.campa: He writes in the one-room summerhouse at the west end of the garden, and receives there whoever comes to the gate. Visitors describe a small old man in a plain coat, courteous, hard of hearing, and entirely willing to be asked about the dead. He eats little, drinks his coffee heavily sweetened, sleeps at irregular hours, and speaks of angels the way another man speaks of colleagues. The Stockholm that will one day interrogate his followers for heresy currently regards him as a distinguished eccentric with a good garden.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, from Tafel's Documents Concerning the Life and Character of Emanuel Swedenborg
suggested_refs: The summerhouse at the west end of the Hornsgatan garden

stops.name: London, Heaven and Hell
stops.date_confidence: attested to London 1758 by swedenborg.com and Wikipedia as one of five concise theological works published there that year; month not given, defaulted to 01. The quotation is verbatim from Heaven and Hell section 59 in the Project Gutenberg English text (ebook 17368). Blake's Marriage of Heaven and Hell is dated to 1790 by the standard record and is named here as later reception, not as a scene.
stops.campa: Five small books come out in London in a single year, and one of them travels: Heaven and Its Wonders and Hell, from Things Heard and Seen. It describes a heaven organized as one human form, angels who were all of them once men, a hell nobody is sentenced to and everybody chooses, and a state after death in which a person becomes outwardly what he already loved. It is written flat, in numbered paragraphs, with no poetry in it at all. William Blake will answer it by title, thirty-two years later.
stops.quote: Heaven in its whole complex reflects a single man
stops.quote_source: Emanuel Swedenborg, Heaven and Its Wonders and Hell, section 59, Project Gutenberg ebook 17368
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 17368, Heaven and Hell
suggested_refs: De caelo et ejus mirabilibus et de inferno, London, 1758
Xul Solar and Jorge Luis Borges in Buenos Aires reading Blake and Swedenborg as reporters rather than poets, per xul_solar.journey.json

segments.name: The Fire, the Receipt, and the Queen's Secret

stops.name: Gothenburg, William Castel's house
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the clairvoyance, [A] as to the fire. The Stockholm fire is independently documented as the Mariabranden, which broke out 19 July 1759 and was extinguished the evening of the 20th (sv.wikipedia; en.wikipedia gives 'Thursday, 19 July 1759'). Kant's letter to Charlotte von Knobloch, which I read at en.wikisource, dates his arrival at Gothenburg to 'towards the end of September' 1759: the year agrees with the record and only the month is wrong, a slip in a letter reconstructing second-hand report years afterwards. The research pool presented July and September as rival dates of equal weight; they are not. City-level coordinate.
stops.campa: He has landed from England at four in the afternoon and is at dinner with fifteen people at William Castel's house when he goes out into the garden and comes back pale. There is a fire in Stockholm, he says, four hundred kilometres away, in Sodermalm, and it is running toward his own house. He goes out again and returns at eight, and tells the room the fire is out, three doors short of his own. Couriers over the following two days bring accounts that match. Immanuel Kant, in Konigsberg, pays a friend to travel to Gothenburg and take statements from the people who were at that table.
stops.quote: Thank God! the fire is extinguished; the third door from my house.
stops.quote_source: Immanuel Kant, letter to Charlotte von Knobloch (1763), in Dreams of a Spirit-Seer, Appendix 2, English translation at Wikisource
sources: Immanuel Kant, letter to Charlotte von Knobloch, en.wikisource.org, 'Dreams of a Spirit-Seer/Appendix 2'
suggested_refs: The Mariabranden of 19-20 July 1759 on Sodermalm, Stockholm

stops.name: Stockholm, the widow Marteville and the receipt
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Kant's own account, the earliest substantial one, names Madame Marteville, widow of the Dutch ambassador, and the goldsmith Croon as the creditor; the research pool's claim that sources differ over whether the ambassador was Dutch or French overstates the disagreement. Kant gives no date at all, so the 1760 year is inference and the month and day are defaults. The quotation is verbatim from Tafel's 1847 edition, Part II ch. XIV, p. 94, not the 1841 edition the pool first cited, whose Marteville pages contain no mention of Bayle; the ultimate source is Thiebault's Souvenirs (1804), relaying Chamberlain d'Hamon.
stops.campa: The widow of the Dutch ambassador Marteville is being pressed by a goldsmith named Croon for payment on a silver service she is certain her husband settled before he died. She asks Swedenborg. The account of what follows is Kant's, written up years afterwards from second-hand report, and the debt and the document are the only parts of it a record can carry. Some days later he tells her the hour at which her husband took the receipt, and what article of Bayle's Dictionary he was reading as he did it, and where the paper is lying in a hidden compartment of a bureau. The receipt is found where he says.
stops.quote: her deceased husband had taken the shopkeeper's receipt for the money on such a day, at such an hour, as he was reading such an article in Bayle's Dictionary in his cabinet
stops.quote_source: R. L. Tafel, Documents Concerning the Life and Character of Emanuel Swedenborg, 1847 edition, Part II ch. XIV, p. 94, relaying Thiebault via Chamberlain d'Hamon
sources: R. L. Tafel, Documents (1847 ed.), Part II ch. XIV, archive.org: documentsconcern00tafe
Dieudonne Thiebault, Souvenirs de vingt ans de sejour a Berlin, vol. II (1804), pp. 254ff.
Immanuel Kant, letter to Charlotte von Knobloch, Wikisource

stops.name: Stockholm, Riddarhuset: the memorial on the exchange
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The November 1760 parliamentary memorial on currency and exchange is carried by the dossier from newchurchhistory.org's reproduction of its structure and was not independently refetched in this pass. The day is not given and defaults to 01. The coordinate is the Riddarhuset, where the noble estate sat.
stops.campa: The daler has been falling for years against the Hamburg exchange and the Riksdag argues about the reason. Swedenborg lays a memorial before the House of Nobility: the cause is the volume of paper credit, the remedy is metallic discipline, and no political arrangement will make a note worth more than what stands behind it. He is seventy-two, and has been publishing accounts of conversations with angels for eleven years. The House of Nobility receives the currency paper as a currency paper.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, citing newchurchhistory.org's reproduction of the November 1760 memorial
suggested_refs: Swedenborg's Riksdag memorial on the exchange rate, November 1760

stops.name: Stockholm, the royal palace: the queen's brother
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The episode circulates through Thiebault's account of Frederick the Great's court and through the queen's own later remarks, collected in Tafel; the quotation is verbatim from the 1847 edition, Part II ch. XIV, p. 95, where it belongs to this episode and not, as the research pool had it, to the Marteville affair. The date is loose across sources, given variously as circa 1758-61; 1761 is used as a sort key. The content of what he said was never recorded by anybody, which is why the claim is unfalsifiable rather than merely unverified.
stops.campa: Queen Louisa Ulrika, sister of Frederick the Great, asks him at court to bring her word from her dead brother Augustus William. He comes back some days later, finds her seated at cards, and says he cannot deliver the errand in front of witnesses. She takes him aside to a window and posts Senator von Schwerin at the door. She turns white and says afterwards that no living person could have told him this. What he actually said to her at that window was never written down.
stops.quote: he could not disclose his errand in the presence of witnesses
stops.quote_source: R. L. Tafel, Documents Concerning the Life and Character of Emanuel Swedenborg, 1847 edition, Part II ch. XIV, p. 95
sources: R. L. Tafel, Documents (1847 ed.), Part II ch. XIV, archive.org: documentsconcern00tafe
Immanuel Kant, letter to Charlotte von Knobloch, Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Stockholm royal palace, and the unrecorded sentence that made the queen turn pale

segments.name: The Books Under His Own Name

stops.name: Amsterdam, Divine Love and Wisdom
stops.date_confidence: Sapientia angelica de Divino Amore et de Divina Sapientia is attested to Amsterdam 1763 and Divina Providentia to Amsterdam 1764 by swedenborg.com's life chronology; Apocalypsis Revelata to Amsterdam 1766. Months are not given and default to 01. Kant's purchase and reading of Arcana Coelestia and his 1766 publication of Traume eines Geistersehers at Konigsberg are attested by Wikipedia; the Konigsberg scene itself belongs to kant.journey.json and is not staged here.
stops.campa: He is publishing steadily out of Amsterdam now, a book or two a year in Latin and at his own expense: Divine Love and Wisdom this year, Divine Providence the next, the Apocalypse Revealed three years after that. The system hardens into doctrine. God is love and wisdom in one, creation descends by degrees from the spiritual into the natural, and every natural thing corresponds to a spiritual thing as an effect corresponds to its cause. In 1766 Immanuel Kant, who has bought the eight volumes and read them, publishes a book laughing at him.
suggested_refs: Sapientia angelica de Divino Amore et de Divina Sapientia, Amsterdam, 1763
Kant's Traume eines Geistersehers, Konigsberg, 1766, and the private inquiries that preceded it

stops.name: Amsterdam, Conjugial Love, with his name on it
stops.date_confidence: attested to Amsterdam 1768 by swedenborg.com, which calls it the first of his theological books to bear his name. The month is not given and defaults to 01. The quotation is verbatim from section 1 of the Project Gutenberg English text (ebook 11248). Chapman's holding of the marriage-after-death doctrine is reported as tradition in johnny_appleseed.journey.json, not as record, and is named here as later reception only.
stops.campa: For twenty years he has printed anonymously. At eighty he puts his name on a title page. The Delights of Wisdom Pertaining to Conjugial Love argues that marriage is not dissolved by death, that a true pair go on afterwards as one angel, and that anyone who has not found the partner on earth will be given one beyond it. The same book carries a long discussion of when a concubine may be tolerated, and Sweden's clergy read that part first. The doctrine of marriage after death is held plainly and acted on, sixty years later, by an unmarried nurseryman in Ohio named John Chapman.
stops.quote: I am aware that many who read the following pages and the Memorable Relations annexed to the chapters, will believe that they are fictions of the imagination; but I solemnly declare they are not fictions, but were truly done and seen
stops.quote_source: Emanuel Swedenborg, The Delights of Wisdom Pertaining to Conjugial Love, section 1, Project Gutenberg ebook 11248
sources: johnny_appleseed.journey.json, on Chapman's marriage-after-death belief as reported tradition
suggested_refs: Delitiae sapientiae de amore conjugiali, Amsterdam, 1768, the first title page to carry his name

stops.name: Gothenburg, the Consistory's complaint
stops.date_confidence: the complaint is dated 27 September 1768 by swedenborgdigitallibrary.org's Swedenborg Epic ch. 41, which also names Bishop Eric Lamberg, Dean Olof Ekebom and the prosecuting lawyer Anders Aurell. The research pool gave the proceeding as concluding in 1770; that is a year short. The Royal Council's final order, that Beyer and Rosen be treated with mildness and Christian charity, is dated 7 December 1771, and the case then passed to the Gota Court of Appeals and stalled. The April 1770 decree condemning the doctrines was an interim step.
stops.campa: A complaint is filed with the Gothenburg Consistory against two men who are not Swedenborg: Gabriel Beyer, a professor, and Johan Rosen, who have been teaching his theology in the town. Dean Olof Ekebom calls the doctrines corrupting and heretical, Bishop Eric Lamberg presides, and the lawyer Anders Aurell prosecutes. The charges are the Trinity, the atonement, justification, and the authority of Scripture. The proceeding runs three years, produces one decree in 1770 and one royal order in 1771, and passes to the Gota Court of Appeals, where it stops without a verdict.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, citing Tafel's collection of the Beyer correspondence
suggested_refs: The Gothenburg Consistory proceedings against Gabriel Beyer and Johan Rosen, 1768-1771

stops.name: Stockholm, the petition to the king
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 May 1770 by swedenborgdigitallibrary.org's Swedenborg Epic ch. 41, which carries the quotation verbatim. The coordinate is the royal palace at Stockholm, where the petition was directed; he was writing from Stockholm at this point in the Epic's account, having written earlier from Amsterdam.
stops.campa: He writes to his king directly on the twenty-fifth of May, an old man of eighty-two asking for protection while two professors stand accused in Gothenburg for teaching what he wrote. He answers the doctrinal charges point by point, and then stops answering them. What he wants set down is not that his theology is orthodox. It is that a member of the House of Nobility, fifty years in his seat and thirty-one in the Board of Mines, has been handled in a way no member of it has been handled before.
stops.quote: I feel compelled at this juncture to have recourse to Your Majesty's protection; for I have been treated as no one has ever been treated before in Sweden.
stops.quote_source: Emanuel Swedenborg, petition to the king, 25 May 1770, quoted in swedenborgdigitallibrary.org, The Swedenborg Epic, ch. 41
suggested_refs: Swedenborg's petition of 25 May 1770 to the Swedish crown

stops.name: Amsterdam, the last book through the press
stops.date_confidence: the July 1770 journey to Amsterdam is attested by Wikipedia; the day is not given and defaults to 01. Publication is a separate fact: swedenborg.com gives the first Latin edition of Vera Christiana Religio as Amsterdam, 1771, and lists True Christianity under 1771 in the life chronology. The research pool collapsed the journey and the publication into 1770 and called it the first book under his own name, which is wrong: Conjugial Love (1768) already carried it. This is the second.
stops.campa: He travels to Amsterdam in July, eighty-two years old, to see the True Christian Religion through the press. It appears the following year with his name on it, the second book to carry it, and it is the whole system in one volume: God, Scripture, faith, charity, baptism, the Holy Supper, and the Last Judgment, which he says has already occurred, in the spiritual world, in 1757, unnoticed by anybody on earth. He writes at the end of it that the new church is now beginning. He does not go home to Sweden again.
sources: swedenborg.com, writings chronology, first Latin edition Amsterdam 1771
suggested_refs: Vera Christiana Religio, Amsterdam, 1771

stops.name: London, Great Bath Street
stops.date_confidence: the 1771 London lodging with Richard Shearsmith, peruke-maker, in Great Bath Street, Coldbath Fields, is attested by Wikipedia; the month of arrival is not given and defaults to 01. The coordinate is corrected from the research pool's 51.527, -0.1107, which lands in Amwell some 350-400 metres north of the historic Coldbath Fields; Great Bath Street ran off Coldbath Square around present-day Mount Pleasant. The street no longer exists, so the pin is an area approximation.
stops.campa: He takes a room with Richard Shearsmith, a wigmaker, in Great Bath Street off Coldbath Fields, north of the city. He is in his eighty-fourth year, at work on a continuation of the True Christian Religion, and receives Swedish visitors who find him lucid, cheerful, and entirely unwilling to argue with anybody. The Shearsmith household will give evidence about him afterwards to the men collecting documents on his life, which is how the ordinary details of these last months survive. Great Bath Street is no longer on the map of London.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, from Tafel's Documents and Sigstedt
suggested_refs: Shearsmith's house, Great Bath Street, Coldbath Fields, a street since erased from the map

stops.name: London, the stroke before Christmas
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1771, shortly before Christmas, by Wikipedia and swedenborg.com; the exact day is not given and defaults to 01. That Arvid Ferelius, the Swedish pastor in London, attended him and administered communion is carried by the dossier's synthesis of Tafel and Sigstedt. The much-repeated deathbed exchange in which he is asked to retract his writings is not in the material verified for this file and is deliberately not written into the campa.
stops.campa: Shortly before Christmas he has a stroke. It leaves him partly paralysed and unable to speak, and for a stretch of weeks he lies there taking almost nothing. Then he recovers enough to talk, to eat, and to receive callers again, and recovers no further than that. Arvid Ferelius, the Swedish pastor in London, comes to the house and administers the sacrament to him. He is eighty-three years old and has been in England, on this last crossing, only since the autumn.
sources: Colegio Invisible dossier, from Tafel's Documents
suggested_refs: Arvid Ferelius, pastor of the Swedish church in London, at the sickbed

stops.name: London, death on a Sunday
stops.date_confidence: attested to Sunday 29 March 1772 by swedenborg.com, Wikipedia and the Swedenborg Society, three independent sources in agreement. No autopsy is documented and stroke complications are given as the probable cause, which is an inference the sources make and not a coroner's finding.
stops.campa: He dies in the Shearsmith house on Sunday the twenty-ninth of March, in his eighty-fifth year. No autopsy is recorded and no physician's account survives; the December stroke and its complications are what the record leaves anybody to reason from. He leaves no wife and no children, and no church that he founded or authorised. He leaves roughly thirty volumes in Latin, most of them printed at his own expense, and perhaps a few dozen serious readers in England. The continuation he had been working on all winter stays unfinished.
suggested_refs: The unfinished continuation of the True Christian Religion, left in the room

stops.name: Shadwell, the Swedish church at Princes Square
stops.date_confidence: burial at the Swedish church, Princes Square, Shadwell, on 5 April 1772 is attested by the Swedenborg Society; Wikipedia describes the same location as Wapping, which is a neighbouring designation for the same ground rather than a conflicting claim. The church was later demolished; the research pool could not corroborate the renaming of the square from a fetched source, so that detail is carried as report. The New Church founding on 7 May 1787 is attested by Wikipedia's article on the General Conference.
stops.campa: He is buried on the fifth of April in the Swedish Lutheran church at Princes Square, Shadwell, the parish of the Swedish sailors and merchants working the port of London, a few streets up from the river. A Swedish parish on English ground is roughly the position he has occupied for thirty years. Fifteen years later, readers of the books will constitute a church in this same city and call it the New Jerusalem. He had ordained nobody and written no order of service for them to use.
sources: Wikipedia, 'General Conference of the New Church'
suggested_refs: The Swedish church at Princes Square, Shadwell, demolished in the following century

stops.name: Stockholm, twenty thousand pages to the Academy
stops.date_confidence: UNESCO's Memory of the World record attests that the manuscripts were donated by his heirs to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences following his death in 1772 and gives the scale as roughly 20,000 pages. No month is given for the donation; June 1772 is a sort placeholder after the March death and is not a claim about the day. The coordinate is central Stockholm, matching the Academy's premises-less state in the eighteenth century rather than its modern campus.
stops.campa: His heirs send the manuscripts to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences: roughly twenty thousand pages in Latin and Swedish, the drafts of everything published, the indexes, the unfinished continuations, and a private notebook of dreams that nobody yet knows is in the pile. The Academy has no doctrinal interest in any of it. It takes the papers because the man was a member and papers are papers, shelves them, and begins the long work of cataloguing twenty thousand sheets in two languages.
sources: UNESCO, 'Emanuel Swedenborg Collection', Memory of the World record
suggested_refs: The Swedenborg manuscript collection, Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

stops.name: Stockholm, Skansen: the summerhouse moved
stops.date_confidence: swedenborg.com gives 1896 as the year the summerhouse was moved to Skansen; Wikipedia's Skansen article confirms the building is in the museum's collection but supplies no date, so the year rests on a single Swedenborgian-affiliated source. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The one-room summerhouse from the Hornsgatan garden is taken apart, carted across the water to Djurgarden, and set up at Skansen among the farmhouses and cottages the museum is assembling into a picture of Swedish life. It is a garden shed with a window, and it is the room in which most of the theology was written. What was moved is the shell. The acre of orchard, hedge maze and kitchen garden around it stayed where it stood on Sodermalm and went under the city.
suggested_refs: Swedenborg's summerhouse in the Skansen open-air museum, Djurgarden

stops.name: Uppsala Cathedral, the vault
stops.date_confidence: the year is corrected against both figures the research pool offered. sv.wikipedia states the remains were moved in 1908 to the Bielke-Liewen burial vault in Uppsala Cathedral, with the ceremony on 19 May 1908, and en.wikipedia's article on Uppsala Cathedral independently states they were transported from England in 1908. The Swedenborg Society's 1910 and the en.wikipedia Swedenborg article's '1912/1913, the 140th anniversary' are both errors, and the anniversary arithmetic does not work in either case. The dossier's separate claim that a skull was returned to Sweden in 1978 could not be confirmed against any independent source and is left out of the campa.
stops.campa: The Swedish state asks for him back. The remains are lifted out of the ground at Shadwell, carried home aboard a naval vessel, and on the nineteenth of May placed in the Bielke-Liewen vault in Uppsala Cathedral, in the same church that holds Carl Linnaeus. He had lain a hundred and thirty-six years in a foreign sailors' parish as a private eccentric, and is reinterred by a state which has decided he is a national possession. Uppsala is the town he matriculated in at eleven.
sources: sv.wikipedia, 'Emanuel Swedenborg', on the 1908 move and the 19 May ceremony
suggested_refs: The Bielke-Liewen burial vault, Uppsala Cathedral

stops.name: Stockholm, Frescati: Memory of the World
stops.date_confidence: the 2005 inscription and the scale of roughly 20,000 autograph pages are confirmed verbatim at UNESCO's Memory of the World record. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The coordinate is the Academy's modern Frescati premises, opened in 1915, where the archive physically sits today; it is used here deliberately for a 2005 event and is not the coordinate used for the 1740 election or the 1772 donation, both of which predate this building.
stops.campa: UNESCO inscribes the Swedenborg collection at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on the Memory of the World Register: about twenty thousand autograph pages, held unbroken since his heirs handed them across. The listing certifies the archive, its completeness and its provenance. It certifies nothing whatever about heaven. He wrote down everything he claimed to have been shown, in a language scholars read, and left the papers to a scientific academy rather than to a church. Whether that was diffidence about the visions or perfect confidence in them, the papers themselves do not say.
sources: UNESCO, 'Emanuel Swedenborg Collection', Memory of the World record
suggested_refs: The Emanuel Swedenborg Collection, inscribed on the Memory of the World Register, 2005
